replying_to: Replying to LoLA: Low-Rank Linear Attention With Sparse Caching
display_title: Official Review of Submission21684 by Reviewer Rkaa

summary.value: The authors proposes LoLA, a training-free enhancement to linear attention that improves long-term associative memory. It introduces a three-part memory system: (i) a local sliding window for recent key-value pairs, (ii) a sparse global cache for hard-to-recall items, and (iii) a low-rank recurrent hidden state for generic context, which is guided by a self-recall error metric to detect and mitigate memory collisions.

strengths.value: The proposed method is effective at NIAH recall.

weaknesses.value:
1. Limited evaluation: The current evaluation focuses on synthetic task and short-context NLP benchmarks. Could authors also evaluate their method on at least one long-context NLP benchmark, e.g. LongBench [1]?
2. Work related to this paper to be discussed:
   - The authors claim that current hybrid approaches only focus on local information with sliding window attention, which is not true. Could authors discuss the recent hybrid architectures with sparse attention, e.g. B'MOJO [2], Se-Attn [3], HAX [4]?
   - For the minimization of Self-Recall Error (Eq. 10) in the paper, could authors discuss the correlation of their method with recent test-time training method, e.g. GatedDeltaNet [5], TTT [6], Titans [7], Lattice [8]?

[1]. LongBench: A Bilingual, Multitask Benchmark for Long Context Understanding. ACL2024.

[2]. B'MOJO: Hybrid State Space Realizations of Foundation Models with Eidetic and Fading Memory. NeurIPS 2024.

[3]. Expansion Span: Combining Fading Memory and Retrieval in Hybrid State Space Models. NeuS 2025.

[4]. Overcoming Long-Context Limitations of State-Space Models via Context-Dependent Sparse Attention. NeurIPS 2025.

[5]. Gated Delta Networks: Improving Mamba2 with Delta Rule. NeurIPS 2024.

[6]. Learning to (Learn at Test Time): RNNs with Expressive Hidden States. ICML 2025.

[7]. Titans: Learning to Memorize at Test Time. https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.00663

[8]. Lattice: Learning to Efficiently Compress the Memory. CoLM 2025.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Submission21684 by Reviewer Rkaa

comment.value:
Thank you for your review and suggestions. We have updated our draft to incorporate results on LongBench tasks, added a discussion of methods (B’MOJO,Se-Attn, HAX) in the related work, and discussed the correlation of SRE with test-time training methods. We believe these changes will better outline the significance of LoLA  and its position in the field.

**Response to Weakness 1:**
In Appendix C, we added a table benchmarking performance on various LongBench tasks, covering Single-doc QA, Multi-Doc QA, & Few-shot Learning. Similar to our findings on synthetic data, we found that the base subquadratic model (LoLCATs) cannot perform these tasks. Even if we scale the sliding window size to 1536 tokens, the extended LoLCATS+ still fails. With the same total cache size as LoLCATS+ (eta=512, lambda=1024), LoLA shows significant improvement over the base model, despite no additional training. 

Similar to RULER, we cannot perform apples-to-apples comparisons with other distilled models (Llamba, Phi-Mamba, Mamba-in-the-Llama, Hedgehog) as they do not report scores for these tasks. However, Mamba2—when pretrained from scratch on 3.5 T tokens (compared to LoLCATs 40M tokens for distillation)—has shown very high performance here in this domain. In the future, we are excited to see how well LoLA can do if given a better intra-head LA+SWA base model with a similar training budget as Mamba2.

**Response to Weakness 2a:** 
This is true that not all hybrid approaches use SWA. We updated our claim in the 4th introduction paragraph to say that hybrid extensions of linear attention often use SWA, which focuses on local information. Furthermore, we added a paragraph in our related work discussing varying types of hybrid architectures more in-depth, including B’MOJO, Se-Attn, & HAX.

**Response to Weakness 2b:**
The self-recall error is rooted in the same underlying principles as recent test-time training (ttt, not to be confused with TTT [6]) methods, with the same goal of mapping keys to their associated values. Test-time training methods—such as linear attention or methods mentioned above—use a parametric key-to-value map and explicitly optimize the online parameters via some form of gradient descent. Some of these methods also incorporate hybrid attention to boost performance with minimal additional compute.

The SRE follows a similar metric to most differentiable loss functions in ttt. For example, the loss function in DeltaNet is represented as 

$min_{m_t} L(m_t; k_1, ..., k_t, v_1, ..., v_t) = \sum_{i=1}^t  \| m_t(k_i) - v_i \|_2^2$

with all tokens 1 to t are used to compute the gradient. However in LoLA, we use intra-head hybrid attention, meaning we have more control over which tokens are used for the online gradient. We choose a subset of tokens that best fit the parametric structure (in a greedy, streaming manner for efficiency). For example, our work optimizes G_t, the set of tokens in the sparse cache, in the outer objective, 

$min_{G_t} min_{m_t}\sum_{i=1, st. k_i \not\in G_t}^{t-\eta} L(m_t(k_i), v_i),$

for any ttt loss function L.

For example, with linear attention as the ttt method in our work, LoLA estimates the “linear parts’’ of the KV pairs with linear attention and estimates the “nonlinear parts” with sparse attention. As a result, the ideas of LoLA can be used for any parametric family of functions for ttt. Though, the ttt objective should still aim for $m_t(k_t) \approx v_t$ for our exact SRE implementation to be useful.

We have added this discussion in the related work section of the Appendix.

replying_to: Replying to LoLA: Low-Rank Linear Attention With Sparse Caching
display_title: Official Review of Submission21684 by Reviewer rvBY

summary.value: The paper proposes **LoLA**, a *training-free* inference-time augmentation for hybrid sliding-window + linear attention models. LoLA keeps three memory systems: (i) a local sliding-window cache, (ii) a sparse global cache, and (iii) a recurrent linear-attention hidden state. It scores KV pairs using a **self-recall error (SRE)** how poorly linear attention alone can reconstruct a value from its key and promotes “hard” pairs into the sparse cache while easier ones flow into the recurrent state. On synthetic long-context recall (RULER/S-NIAH) and some zero-shot commonsense tasks, LoLA improves over the authors’ distilled LoLCATs baselines under fixed cache budgets.

strengths.value: The SRE criterion is intuitive and easy to compute given $\Phi(k)$, H, s; the paper supplies pseudo-code and a useful efficiency study (TTFT and VRAM) versus sliding-window size η and sparse-cache size $\lambda$, which practitioners can adopt to tune deployments.

weaknesses.value:
1. **Positioning / novelty is narrow and tied to a special base model.** Although billed as “training-free,” LoLA **assumes** a specific *subquadratic* base (sliding-window + linear attention) obtained via distillation/LoRA (40M tokens) before LoLA can be used. It is therefore not a drop-in for standard Transformers and the headline “training-free” risks misinterpretation. Please clarify scope and re-title accordingly; also separate the cost/benefit of distillation from LoLA’s cache policy.  

2. **Claims vs. baselines and calculation clarity.** The abstract’s “**4.6$\times$ smaller cache than Llama-3.1-8B on 4K**” is not explained precisely; Table 1 lists the Transformer as full-attention (effectively a 4K-token KV cache at 4K), while LoLA uses η+λ (e.g., 256+256). Please specify exactly which Llama cache size is used for that factor and how it’s computed; as written, it’s hard to reconcile. More broadly, comparisons mix distilled subquadratic models and different training budgets; ensure apples-to-apples controls (same teacher, tokens, and evaluation protocol).   

3. **Evidence focuses on synthetic recall; limited breadth on real tasks and ablations.** The large wins are concentrated on RULER/S-NIAH; while there are commonsense results, the absolute gains vs. LoLCATs are modest in places and still trail Llama on some tasks. Scoring ablations for SRE are shown but only on S-NIAH @ 0.5K; please broaden ablations (e.g., alternative importance metrics, cache-update cadence, chunk size sensitivity) on harder and real-world long-context tasks (multi-needle, multi-hop QA with citations).

questions.value:
* **Grammar in Fig. caption.** “**LoLA stores past KV pairs in three forms memory**” → *three forms of memory*. 
* **Informal wording.** “**anyways**” → *anyway*. (Figure text) 
* **Spelling.** “**pruple**” → *purple*. (Figure text) 
* **Apostrophe.** “**Its more efficient**” → *It’s more efficient*. (Figure text) 
* **Spelling.** “**occurence**” → *occurrence*. (Appendix F text) 
* **Consistency.** Use either *commonsense* or *common sense* uniformly; currently the abstract uses “commonsense” while Table 3 caption uses “common sense.”  
* **Section label consistency.** TOC line says “**Algorithm Psuedo-code**” (again typo); ensure capitalization and spelling consistent with the section header. 
* Reframe “training-free” to “inference-only augmentation **for subquadratic models**” and clearly delineate the *pre-training/distillation* of the base from the *LoLA* mechanism. Provide a small *plug-compatibility* study across multiple linear-attention bases to evidence generality. 
* Make the cache-size factor claims auditable: define the exact KV token counts behind “× smaller” in each table/setting, and add a per-token throughput plot (not only TTFT) with and without sparse rescoring, end-to-end (I/O included).

comment.value:
Thank you for your time spent reviewing our work. We made numerous changes to our manuscript: fixing typos, changing the scope around “training-free”, adding another long context benchmark on real data, extending the related work, and adjusting our language to better emphasize our ablations. We believe these updates have strengthened our work. As mentioned below, we will be adding a model throughput plot shortly. 

**Response to Q1,5,6,7:** Thank you for catching these writing errors. We updated these accordingly.

**Response to Q2,3,4:**
These words (e.g. “pruple”) do not exist in our paper. If we missed something, we would appreciate it if you could point us to the exact location in the paper. 

**Response to Q8**: 

>"Reframe “training-free” to “inference-only augmentation for subquadratic models” and clearly delineate the pre-training/distillation of the base from the LoLA mechanism."

We removed the “training-free” terminology in the updated draft and now use “inference-only augmentation” instead. We also changed our wording to emphasize that the LoLA mechanism is largely agnostic to the way the base hybrid attention model was trained. 

>"Provide a small plug-compatibility study across multiple linear-attention bases to evidence generality." 

Regarding the suggested “plug-compatibility” study, we agree that testing on other LA approaches would be a useful experiment to improve the confidence of practitioners with our method. However, with limited resources, we cannot train multiple new hybrid linear attention models from scratch, especially in the rebuttal period. We originally made this trade off to showcase results with scale on a large model with distillation rather than small models via pretraining. We ultimately leave this to future work when we get more computing resources. While only tested on LoLCATs, we believe our paper is an impactful first step towards the use of SRE in future methods.

**Response to W1:**

>“Although billed as “training-free,” LoLA assumes a specific subquadratic base (sliding-window + linear attention) obtained via distillation/LoRA (40M tokens) before LoLA can be used."

We updated Section 4 to emphasize that the cost/benefit of distillation is not tied to LoLA. Distillation improves the base model and is not a contribution of our work. The LoLA mechanism does not assume anything about how the underlying base model was trained; LoLA only assumes the architecture structure (intra-head sliding window + linear attention). As an inference strategy, LoLA just improves the performance of an already trained model.

>"It is therefore not a drop-in for standard Transformers and the headline “training-free” risks misinterpretation. Please clarify scope and re-title accordingly; also separate the cost/benefit of distillation from LoLA’s cache policy.”

In our abstract, we state that LoLA is an inference strategy for linear attention models and do not present it as an inference time drop-in replacement to traditional transformers. We do not believe our current title, “LoLA: Low-Rank Linear Attention with Sparse Caching“, implies this either. We would prefer not to re-title.

We revised our manuscript, removing the phrase “training-free” as mentioned above and emphasized the scope of our paper as an inference augmentation to linear attention models.

**Response to W2 + Q9**:

>“Claims vs. baselines and calculation clarity. The abstract’s “4.6x smaller cache than Llama-3.1-8B on 4K” is not explained precisely; Table 1 lists the Transformer as full-attention (effectively a 4K-token KV cache at 4K), while LoLA uses η+λ (e.g., 256+256). Please specify exactly which Llama cache size is used for that factor and how it’s computed; as written, it’s hard to reconcile. More broadly, comparisons mix distilled subquadratic models and different training budgets; ensure apples-to-apples controls (same teacher, tokens, and evaluation protocol).”

>“Make the cache-size factor claims auditable: define the exact KV token counts behind “× smaller” in each table/setting, and add a per-token throughput plot (not only TTFT) with and without sparse rescoring, end-to-end (I/O included).”

We updated Appendix B to explain how LoLAs cache size is calculated for Figure 7. Since Llama is a transformer, using full-attention as you mentioned, 4K tokens implies the cache is holding 4K key-value pairs. We divided the number of elements in LoLAs cache at eta=lambda=256 with the number of elements a transformer stores at 4K context length.

Additionally, we will be adding a per-token throughput information in Appendix B as well to satisfy Q9. Since the TTFT is similar to the prefill or training throughput, we will provide the number of tokens generated per second when decoding. 

Our original presentation of the TTFT plot did not fully explain the “without sparse rescoring” setting. This occurs when lambda=0, as the sparse cache holds 0 tokens, so nothing is rescored. We updated our language in Appendix B to explicitly state this to avoid ambiguity.

“More broadly, comparisons mix distilled subquadratic models and different training budgets; ensure apples-to-apples controls (same teacher, tokens, and evaluation protocol).”

We aimed to provide apples-to-apples comparisons with LoLCATs+ (an extended sliding window version with the same total cache size). We also provide results from other architectures (with varying training budgets) and list how many tokens they were trained on, along with what kind of tokens (distilled or raw data) for full transparency. When possible, in our tables, we grouped models by similar pretraining sources.

**Response to W3**:
>“Evidence focuses on synthetic recall; limited breadth on real tasks and ablations.” 

>“please broaden ablations (e.g., alternative importance metrics, cache-update cadence, chunk size sensitivity)”

Thank you for the suggestion. We added new results on LongBench tasks in Appendix C to cover more real world long context tasks. 

While we were only explicit about ablating alternative importance metrics in Section 4.3 (and Appendix F), we indirectly provided results in Appendix B on variable tracking (a much harder task than S-NIAH) for various cache parameters (eta, lambda). Remember, eta controls the cache-update cadence and chunksize. 

In our updated draft, we emphasize this extended ablation by changing language at the end of Section 3 and Appendix B.  In this cache parameter ablation, we chose variable tracking due to its difficulty with sparse approaches. Variable tracking requires modeling the whole context, not just the most important tokens. We found that the model completely fails on this task without sparse caching (lambda=0). With at least moderate sized sparse cache, we achieve quite high scores. Additionally, while moderate chunk sizes performed the best, the largest eta, which has slower update cadence, achieved slightly reduced scores. Overall, sparse caches that model the whole context are essential on this harder task. 


“The large wins are concentrated on RULER/S-NIAH; while there are commonsense results, the absolute gains vs. LoLCATs are modest in places and still trail Llama on some tasks.”

We appreciate that you found the long context results to be a large win. We agree commonsense results are more modest because linear attention does not face as many memory collisions in a short context. LoLCATs approach excels over other base models in this domain, but completely fails in a long context. We demonstrate that LoLA can enable long context performance while still matching or exceeding such high short context for subquadratic models.

While you stated that LoLA “still trail[s] Llama on some tasks”, we find that matching Llama is a huge win since LoLA is a bounded inference cost alternative to transformers. We would also like to emphasize that in the 1B parameter setting, our inference strategy actually shows improvements beyond Llama-3.2-1B for commonsense tasks, seen in Appendix A. We found this result to be quite exciting.

As promised, we added a per-token throughput table during decoding in Appendix B, satisfying Q9. While a large chunk size is important for fast prefill and training, we observe that decoding throughput is less sensitive to varying cache parameters.

display_title: Official Review of Submission21684 by Reviewer 4qjE

summary.value: This paper introduces LoLA, a training-free inference strategy designed to solve the poor memory capacity of linear attention models. Standard linear attention suffers from "memory collisions," where new information overwrites past associations in its fixed-size hidden state. LoLA addresses this by augmenting hybrid linear attention models with a novel three-part memory system: (i) a local sliding window cache for recent key-value (KV) pairs, (ii) a sparse, global cache for difficult-to-memorize pairs, and (iii) the standard recurrent hidden state for all other generic pairs. The core of LoLA is a new importance metric called Self-Recall Error (SRE), which is used to manage the sparse cache. SRE measures how well the current linear hidden state can already retrieve a KV pair's correct value. Pairs that are difficult to recall (high SRE) are kept in the full-rank sparse cache to prevent them from being corrupted, while easy-to-recall pairs (low SRE) are compressed into the hidden state. This method is highly effective, improving a base model's accuracy on pass-key retrieval tasks from 0.6% to 97.4% and achieving strong performance on general commonsense reasoning benchmarks.

strengths.value:
1. The paper's core idea is highly original. Instead of using query similarity or softmax scores for sparse attention, it introduces the Self Recall Error (SRE) . This query agnostic metric provides a principled, data driven way to determine which tokens are "difficult to memorize" for the linear state and should be cached in full rank. This is a clever and novel approach to mitigating memory collisions.

2. The claims are supported by exceptionally strong and well targeted experiments. The method provides a near perfect fix for associative recall on Needle in a Haystack (NIAH) tasks, boosting accuracy from a failing 0.6% to 97.4%. Furthermore, the ablation study in Table 4 is critical, proving that LoLA's SRE metric (99.0% accuracy) is vastly superior to intuitive alternatives like extending the sliding window (29.4%) or using other sparse attention metrics (e.g., 11.4%, 20.0%).

3. The work is highly significant because it is a training free inference strategy. This allows it to be applied directly to existing, pretrained hybrid models like LoLCATs to immediately unlock their long context recall capabilities.

weaknesses.value:
1. The paper states the scoring introduces a "small overhead compute cost". However, the proposed algorithm re-scores all $\lambda$ elements in the sparse cache plus the new candidate token(s) at every generation step. This overhead is non trivial, especially when $\lambda$ is large. The Time to First Token (TTFT) in Figure 4 confirms this. For a 64 token window, TTFT increases from 0.99s ($\lambda=0$) to 1.46s ($\lambda=512$). This is a roughly 47% slowdown. This trade off is not sufficiently addressed in the main paper.

2. The paper positions LoLA as a solution to memory collisions in linear attention but fails to compare its approach to other architectures designed to solve the exact same problem. Specifically, Gated DeltaNet, a highly relevant model, combines gating and a delta rule to precisely manage its recurrent state, mitigate collisions, and improve associative recall. While Gated DeltaNet is a different architecture (requiring training) and LoLA is an inference strategy, they are both direct solutions to memory collisions. The paper should have discussed, if not benchmarked against, such advanced recurrent models.

3. The method is described as "training free". While true that LoLA itself is an inference strategy, its SRE metric (Equation 10) is entirely dependent on the feature map $\phi$, which was learned during the distillation of the LoLCATs base model. It is unclear if LoLA would be as effective if applied to a linear attention model trained from scratch, or one using a different $\phi$.

questions.value:
1. The paper's goal is to mitigate memory collisions, which is the same goal as advanced recurrent models like Gated DeltaNet. How do the authors view LoLA's "sparse caching" approach in comparison to Gated DeltaNet's "gating + delta rule" approach? 

2. The TTFT analysis in Figure 4 shows a clear slowdown as $\lambda$ increases. Could the authors provide a more direct comparison of this overhead? 

3. The SRE metric relies on the $\phi$ map learned by the LoLCATs base model. Have the authors tested whether LoLA is effective when applied to other linear attention models that were not trained with LoLCATs' specific distillation process, such as a model pretrained from scratch?

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Submission21684 by Reviewer 4qjE

comment.value:
Thank you for finding our query-agnostic metric to be “highly original” and “supported by exceptionally strong and well targeted experiments”. Your review brought up relevant comments about the overhead compute costs, connection to gating / Gated DeltaNet, and relationship between SRE and feature maps. We have made several changes in the paper to incorporate this feedback and improve clarity in the paper. 


**Response to W1:**
We agree this trade off was not sufficiently explained in the main body. In Appendix B, we provided a short guide on how a practitioner should navigate this trade-off depending on their constraints. To address the trade-off in the main work, we updated our draft to include a summary of Appendix B at the end of Section 3.

LoLA re-scores the sparse cache after each chunk of tokens which is controlled by the hyperparameter eta. We have updated our language in Section 3 to clarify the chunkwise updates.

While it is true that small chunks or windows (eta=64) can lead to a slowdown with sparse caching, the relative overhead of sparse caching decreases for moderate chunk sizes (i.e. eta=256 or 512). Figure 5 also shows that such chunk sizes still have feasible VRAM requirements. We now reference  how larger chunk sizes can reduce the overhead cost of sparse caching in Section 3 and Appendix B.

**Question 2:**
“The TTFT analysis in Figure 4 shows a clear slowdown as increases. Could the authors provide a more direct comparison of this overhead?”

In Table 7 (Appendix B) of the updated draft, we added a more direct comparison of this overhead by recording the latency of each layer’s forward pass (for various window/sparse cache sizes), as opposed to the end-to-end TTFT. 


**Response to W2:**
We agree that Gated DeltaNet is a very impactful work in the field. We provided comparisons to Gated DeltaNet in Appendix A and briefly discussed it in our related work in Appendix D. This was not originally in the main body, so we updated the language at the end of section 4.2 to better reference this work. Since the Gated DeltaNet paper uses 1.3B parameter models,  we compare Gated DeltaNet to our 1B model in the Appendix. The results in our main body of this work use 8B parameters to better showcase scale. We also updated our related work to discuss this paper (and other test-time regression work) more in depth. 



**Response to Q1:**

We view these advancements (delta rule, sparse caching, and gating) as relatively orthogonal. Delta rule provides a better online objective (L2 vs dot product loss) for the linear key-to-value estimation. Gating can alleviate some memory collisions by de-prioritizing old information, aka forgetting old information to make room for new information. This is done by using smaller coefficients (gamma) for old KV pairs in the online objective, with

$\sum_i^t \gamma_i^{(t)} \| m(k_i)_t - v_i \|_2^2.$

Sparse caching, on the other hand, allocates the difficult (not necessarily old) memories to sparse attention. More information is preserved across the hybrid attention mechanism. While gating can improve linear attention in isolation, the linear hidden state is still limited by memory capacity (proportional to dimensionality). Nonlinear associative systems, either through hybrid attention (LoLA) or nonlinear maps, are required for superlinear capacity. 

Along with our comments in W2, we have updated the related work to discuss Gated DeltaNet (and its  relationship to sparse caching) more in depth.

replying_to: Replying to Official Comment by Authors

comment.value:
**Response to Weakness 3 / Q3:**

Thank you for bringing this up, we have updated Eq. 10 to avoid confusion on the relationship between feature maps and SRE. The updated Eq. 10 defines the SRE as
$SRE(k,v,m_t) = \| m_t(k) - v\|_2.$
Then, for the particular case of feature maps + normalization (i.e. LoLCATs), this will be implemented as 
	$\| \frac{\phi(k)H_t}{\phi(k)s_t}- v\|_2.$
following Eq. 9. This revised language emphasizes that self-recall error can be implemented with any test-time training approach. LoLCATs/Hedgehogs’ feature map does not have any special connection to computing the SRE. 

As a result, we believe SRE to be useful for other linear attention models (pretrained from scratch and/or without feature maps). Memory collisions are a critical flaw of linear attention; the memory capacity will always be limited by the dimensionality of the hidden state. The SRE identifies when this happens. We acknowledge this concern and have updated our manuscript in section 3. Furthermore, since the feature map inflates the hidden state dimensionality, removing this could make sparse caching more crucial. For example, we have observed caching to be more useful on small base models with smaller dimensional keys in Appendix A.

We have not tested LoLA for non-LoLCATs models particularly due to the compute cost of pretraining language models from scratch. This is what drew us to use LoLCATs as the base model in the first place. We agree that testing on other LA approaches would be a useful experiment to improve the confidence of practitioners with our method. We made this trade off to showcase results on large models with distillation rather than small models with pretraining. We ultimately leave this to future work when we get more computing resources. While only tested on LoLCATs, we believe our paper is an impactful first step towards the use of SRE in future methods.

To avoid any concerns or confusion about the “training-free” terminology, we removed this entirely from the manuscript.

summary.value: The paper introduces LoLA, a training-free inference strategy that enhances linear attention models by mitigating their poor memory capacity. It distributes key-value pairs into three systems: a local sliding window, the low-rank recurrent state, and a new sparse global cache that stores "difficult-to-memorize" pairs identified by a self-recall error metric, drastically improving associative recall.

strengths.value:
1. The paper empirically demonstrates an improvement on tasks where the base model completely fails
2. The propose of a new sparse global cache is novel

weaknesses.value:
1. The method adds a new computational cost not present in standard linear attention, specifically for scoring and managing the sparse cache. The paper says its overhead is O(λd) which itself needs to be larger for more complex, long-context tasks.
2. LoLA moves away from the simplicity of linear attention by requiring three distinct memory systems that must be managed. 
3.  This caching strategy cannot fully compensate for the knowledge lost during the base model's efficient distillation from attention

comment.value:
We appreciate your careful review of the paper. We have added some clarifying remarks in our manuscript about the complexity tradeoff, knowledge loss in the base model, and linear attention latencies.

**Response to Weaknesses 1 and 2:**
These are valid concerns. Although LoLA increases complexity, the original LA’s performance is far too low to be useful for long context. We must trade a small increase in compute and complexity to enable long context recall. As you mentioned, the base linear attention model (even with an additional sliding window) completely fails in such settings. To clarify this point, we updated the 3rd introduction paragraph to better motivate why linear attention alone, despite its simplicity and efficiency, is insufficient.

**Response to Weakness 3:**
We agree that our inference augmentation can not completely repair the downsides of the base subquadratic model. At the end of section 2.3, we added a sentence to remind the readers of knowledge loss during the base model’s efficient distillation for transparency.


**Response to Question 1:**
Yes, we updated our discussion of Figure 4 in Appendix B to include an exact comparison.  Additionally, lambda=0 showcases latency for LA+SWA; however, we did not make this clear. We updated this language alongside the LA latency results.
